title: Market structures
examples: What is the main difference between perfect competition and monopoly?
Can you give an example of an oligopoly in our local area?
How does the number of sellers affect the market price?

explain.say: Today we will explore different market structures. These structures describe how many firms operate in a market. We will look at four main types today.

items: Perfect Competition: Many sellers, no single control.
Monopolistic Competition: Many sellers, differentiated products.
Monopoly: One seller, total market control.

explain.say: Perfect competition has many small sellers selling identical products. Think of a local market stall selling basic vegetables. No single farmer can control the price.
Monopolistic competition has many firms, but they sell slightly different goods. Think of local restaurants offering unique menus. They try to differentiate their offerings.
An oligopoly involves only a few large firms dominating the market. Consider the mobile phone service providers in a country. They are few and watch each other closely.
A pure monopoly means only one firm supplies the entire market. Think of a utility company providing water services in a town. They often have legal protection.
In the real world, the local electricity market shows oligopolistic tendencies. A few large generators control the supply, making them interdependent.

faq.q: What is the main difference between oligopoly and perfect competition?
faq.a: In perfect competition, there are many sellers, so no one controls the price. In an oligopoly, there are only a few sellers, and their actions affect each other greatly.
asks: Are the sellers independent in perfect competition?
How does interdependence work in oligopoly?

faq.q: Does monopolistic competition mean products are completely unique?
faq.a: No, it means they are differentiated, so they are not exactly the same. They are close substitutes but have unique branding or features.
asks: Can I use this for clothing brands?

faq.q: What are the barriers to entry in a natural monopoly?
faq.a: Barriers are obstacles that prevent new firms from entering the market. These can be legal restrictions or huge setup costs.
asks: What stops a new company from starting?
Are patents a type of barrier?

faq.q: If I am in a perfect competition market, can I raise my price?
faq.a: No, because you are one of many identical sellers, raising your price will cause customers to simply buy from a competitor instead.
asks: Do I have pricing power in perfect competition?
Who sets the price in this market?

faq.q: Are the four structures always present in the real world?
faq.a: No, most real-world markets are a mix or lean towards one extreme. For example, technology markets often show oligopolistic traits.
asks: Can a market be perfectly competitive?
Which structure is the most common?

facts: Perfect competition assumes all buyers and sellers are price takers.
Monopolistic competition relies on product differentiation to gain market share.
An oligopoly is characterized by mutual interdependence among the few firms.
A pure monopoly usually exists due to high barriers to entry.

quiz.say: A market with only two major airlines competing for passengers is an example of:
quiz.why: Because there are only a few large firms, their pricing decisions affect the others greatly.

wrong.0: A monopoly requires only one seller in the entire market.
wrong.1: This structure involves many sellers with slightly different products.
wrong.3: This implies many sellers, not just two major airlines.

quiz.say: If a local bakery sells bread that is very similar to every other bakery, but uses a unique local recipe, what structure is it closest to?
quiz.why: The many sellers suggest competition, but the unique recipe shows differentiation.

wrong.1: This would require the bread to be completely identical to all others.
wrong.2: This structure requires only a few dominant sellers.
wrong.3: This suggests only one bakery exists in the entire town.

quiz.say: Which market structure has the lowest barriers to entry?
quiz.why: The assumption of low barriers allows many new firms to enter easily.

wrong.1: A monopoly is defined by having very high barriers to entry.
wrong.2: While barriers exist, the focus is on the small number of firms.
wrong.3: While barriers are lower than monopoly, they are usually higher than in perfect competition.
